title: I Spent 6 Months Building a Physics-Based Hiking Simulator with AI — Some Experiences and Limitations
author: pulsarlab
selftext:
I'm an experienced hiker and an algorithm engineer based in Shenzhen, China, working for a US multinational company.  
I've personally experienced getting lost, dangerous falls, and the risk of hypothermia while hiking. These experiences taught me that bringing too little equipment can be dangerous, but carrying too much gear can also add unnecessary weight and increase the risks.  
Initially, I just wanted to build a hiking simulator, not a game. It didn't even have fancy graphics. My goal was to let people experiment with different equipment choices on real hiking trails and understand the potential consequences of those decisions.  
I even used the simulator to recreate two real-world hiking disasters: the Savage-Lundy Loop incident and the Gansu ultramarathon tragedy. The simulation results were remarkably close to what actually happened, including the locations where the incidents occurred.  
However, when I started testing the simulator with other people, I found that there wasn't much interest in it.  
Later, when GPT-6 was released, I realized that AI had become capable of producing much better visuals. So I started turning the simulator into an actual game.  
**What Has AI Helped Me Accomplish?**  
I've been working on this project for about six months, mainly using Claude, GPT, and DeepSeek to assist with development. At one point, I was using five Pro subscriptions per month.  
My estimate is that building a system of similar complexity without today's AI tools would have taken me at least three years.  
**1. Complex Physics Simulation**  
The game simulates physical exertion, fatigue, wind chill, moisture, sunlight exposure, body temperature, and other environmental factors, along with their interactions with more than 200 pieces of outdoor equipment.  
To make equipment behavior as realistic as possible, I also had AI analyze around 1,000 outdoor gear reviews and used the information to help calibrate the equipment models.  
**2. Real Hiking Trails**  
The routes in the game aren't fictional. They're generated from real hiking GPX data.  
Players need to plan their expeditions based on terrain, weather, and equipment choices, rather than simply deciding whether to move forward or turn back.  
**3. Game Design Is Still Really Hard**  
This has been my biggest challenge so far.  
AI has helped me implement complex algorithms and systems much faster, but when it comes to gameplay interactions, game feel, visual consistency, and overall game design, I still think there's a significant gap between what AI can produce and what an experienced human development team can achieve.  
In particular, turning a physically realistic simulator into a game that's both fun to play and visually appealing has been much harder than I expected.  
**My Thoughts on the Gaming Community's Resistance to AI-Generated Assets**  
I understand why some gaming communities are against AI-generated assets, but I'd also like to share a different perspective.  
Traditionally, developing a complex hiking simulation game like this would require a significant investment of time and money, with no way of knowing in advance whether there's even a market for the gameplay.  
For an indie developer, it's very difficult to justify spending several years building something before finding out whether anyone actually wants to play it.  
AI has allowed me to turn an idea that might previously have taken years into a testable product in about six months.  
I think the value of AI isn't just that it reduces the cost of making existing types of games. It also makes it possible to explore game concepts that might never have been attempted otherwise.  
**What's Next?**  
I'm planning to release the first playable test version soon.  
If you're interested in hiking, survival simulations, realistic physics systems, or AI-assisted game development, I'd love to connect and exchange ideas.
